title: Even Tree
directAnswer: Root the tree and compute every node's subtree size with a single DFS. You may cut the edge above any non-root node whose subtree has an even number of nodes — doing so peels off an even component and leaves the rest even too. The maximum number of removable edges is simply the count of non-root nodes with an even subtree size. O(V).

remember.pattern: Root the tree, DFS subtree sizes, count even non-root subtrees
remember.formula:
root at 1, compute size[u] = 1 + sum(size[child])
answer = number of nodes u (u != root) with size[u] even
# total nodes N is even, so the leftover is always even too
rules: The total node count `N` is **even** (guaranteed) — that is what makes an all-even partition possible.
You may cut the parent edge of node `u` exactly when `size[u]` is **even**; count every such non-root node.
The **root** has no parent edge, so it never contributes a cut even if `size[root] = N` is even.
Cuts are **independent**: removing one even subtree leaves both pieces even, so greedily taking all of them is optimal.
Use an **iterative** DFS (explicit stack) — a deep or skewed tree can overflow a recursive call stack.
whenToUse: Tree problems answerable from **subtree sizes** computed in one post-order pass
Partitioning a tree by cutting edges under a parity / size constraint
Greedy cut decisions that are locally safe and globally independent
Any 'remove edges so each piece satisfies P' on a tree where P depends only on subtree counts
antiSignals: The graph has cycles → it is not a tree; subtree sizes are undefined
Cuts interact (one affects another's validity) → greedy fails, needs DP
You need an actual minimum or weighted partition → tree DP over (cut, not-cut) states
Constraint depends on node values, not counts → size alone is insufficient
remember.takeaway: Subtree sizes from one DFS answer a surprising range of tree questions. Here, an even subtree can always be detached without harming the rest, so the answer is just how many even subtrees hang below the root — a clean greedy backed by the evenness of N.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you root the tree, see that a single DFS subtree-size pass suffices, and can argue why cutting every even subtree is both valid and maximal — plus whether you make the traversal iterative for large trees.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Counting the root's subtree (it has no parent edge to cut), assuming cuts conflict and reaching for DP, or recursing and overflowing the stack on a skewed tree.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Prove the greedy: cutting an even subtree leaves an even remainder because N is even, so the cuts never interfere. Then note the answer is a plain count of even non-root subtrees, computed in O(V).

problemStatement:
You are given a tree (a connected, acyclic, undirected graph) of `N` nodes labeled `1` to `N`, rooted at node `1`, described by a list of `edges`. `N` is even.

Remove as many edges as possible so that every resulting connected component has an **even** number of nodes. Return the **maximum number of edges** you can remove.
constraints: The graph is a tree: exactly N − 1 edges, connected, acyclic
Nodes are labeled 1 to N, rooted at node 1
Edges are undirected; build the tree by skipping the parent when recursing
A valid partition always exists because N is even
understanding: Rooting the tree at node 1 gives every node (except the root) exactly one parent edge — the only edge you could cut to separate that node's subtree from the rest. Cutting it carves off a component equal to that subtree. For the carved-off piece to be even, the subtree must have an even node count; and because the whole tree has an even count, whatever remains after removing an even piece is also even. So each even subtree is an independently safe cut, and the answer is how many such subtrees exist below the root.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is N guaranteed even?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. If N were odd, no partition into all-even components could exist (the sizes would have to sum to an odd total). Evenness of N is what guarantees a solution.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the input really a tree?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — connected and acyclic with N − 1 edges. That is why every non-root node has a unique parent edge and well-defined subtree.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can cutting one edge make another cut invalid?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Removing an even subtree leaves an even remainder, so other even subtrees stay even. The cuts are independent — that is the heart of the greedy.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the root's subtree count?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. The root has no parent edge, so its (size N) subtree can never be detached. Only non-root even subtrees count.

examples.explanation: Subtree of 3 = {3,4} (size 2) and subtree of 6 = {6,8,9,10} (size 4) are even. Cutting both leaves {1,2,5,7} (size 4). All even → 2 edges removed.
Only node 3 has an even subtree {3,4} (size 2). Cut edge 2–3 → {3,4} and {1,2}, both even. 1 edge.
Each leaf's subtree has size 1 (odd). No even non-root subtree exists, so no edge can be cut.

approaches.name: Recursive DFS Subtree Sizes (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: The clearest way to state the idea: a post-order recursion returns each subtree's size, and you count even ones along the way. Then flag the recursion-depth caveat for large trees.
hints: Root the tree at node 1. What single number per node tells you whether its parent edge is cuttable?
A subtree's size is 1 plus the sizes of its children's subtrees — a textbook post-order recursion.
While returning each size, if it is even and the node is not the root, increment a cut counter.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is visited once and its size computed from its children → O(V) time. The recursion stack can be as deep as the tree height, which is O(V) on a skewed (chain) tree.
approaches.explanation:
Subtree sizes are the whole game, and a post-order DFS computes them in one sweep.

**Why subtree size decides each edge.** In a rooted tree, the only edge that isolates node `u`'s subtree from everything else is the edge from `u` to its parent. Cutting it produces a component that is exactly `u`'s subtree. So that cut is legal — yields an even component — precisely when `size[u]` is even.

**Why the greedy is also maximal.** Suppose you cut the parent edges of every non-root node with an even subtree. Each such cut removes an even-sized piece, and because `N` is even, the part left behind after removing an even piece is still even. So no cut spoils another's validity, and every legal cut can be taken simultaneously. You cannot do better than cutting *every* legal edge, so counting them is optimal.

**Why the root is excluded.** The root has no parent, hence no edge above it to cut. Its subtree (the whole tree, size `N`, which is even) is never a separable piece, so it must not be counted.

**The recursion shape.** `dfs(u, parent)` returns `size(u)`: start at 1, add `dfs(child, u)` for each neighbor that is not the parent, and if the returned size is even and `u` is not the root, bump the counter. Skipping the parent is how an undirected edge list is treated as a rooted tree without a separate visited array.

**The caveat.** On a skewed tree (a long chain), the recursion nests `O(V)` deep. With small `N` here that is safe, but as a habit you should note that a deep tree can overflow the call stack — which motivates the iterative version.
approaches.insight: One post-order pass yields every subtree size, and the cut rule is a one-line parity test. The greedy is justified by N being even: removing an even chunk always leaves an even chunk, so the cuts never collide.

code.python:
import sys

def even_forest(self, n: int, edges: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    adj: list[list[int]] = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    self.cuts = 0
    sys.setrecursionlimit(2 * n + 10)   # guard a deep chain

    def dfs(u: int, parent: int) -> int:
        size = 1
        for v in adj[u]:
            if v != parent:             # skip the edge back to the parent
                size += dfs(v, u)
        if u != 1 and size % 2 == 0:    # even subtree, not the root
            self.cuts += 1
        return size

    dfs(1, 0)
    return self.cuts

approaches.name: Iterative DFS Subtree Sizes (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The production-safe version. Compute a traversal order with an explicit stack, then accumulate sizes in reverse — no recursion, so no stack-overflow risk on a deep tree.
hints: The recursion only used the stack to defer a parent until its children finished. Can you get the same post-order effect without the call stack?
Do an iterative DFS from the root recording parents and a visit order. A node always appears before its children in that order.
Walk the order in REVERSE: each node's children are already processed, so its size is final. Count it if even and non-root, then add its size to its parent.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The forward DFS pushes and pops each node once → O(V). The reverse accumulation visits each node once → O(V). Arrays for parent, size, and the order list are O(V). No recursion stack.
approaches.explanation:
The logic is identical to the recursion; only the mechanism changes so a deep tree cannot blow the call stack.

**Step 1 — order and parents.** Run an iterative DFS (or BFS) from the root using an explicit stack. When you pop a node, append it to an `order` list and push each neighbor that is not its parent, recording the parent as you go. Because the tree is acyclic, each node is pushed exactly once; the parent check replaces a visited array. In the resulting `order`, every node appears *before* all of its descendants.

**Step 2 — sizes in reverse.** Initialize `size[u] = 1` for all nodes. Iterate `order` in reverse. When you reach node `u`, all of its descendants have already been processed, so `size[u]` has already accumulated every child's subtree — it is final. If `u` is not the root and `size[u]` is even, increment the cut count. Then fold `u`'s size into its parent: `size[parent[u]] += size[u]`. By the time you reach any node, its full subtree size is known, exactly mirroring post-order recursion.

**Why this is the safe default.** The only difference from the recursive version is that the deferral lives on an explicit heap-allocated stack and an array sweep, not on the call stack. A chain of `10⁵` nodes — or any skewed tree — processes without risk of overflow. The time and the answer are identical.

**Why the parity rule is unchanged.** Cutting the parent edge of an even subtree still peels off an even component and leaves an even remainder (N is even), so every even non-root subtree is an independent, valid, and necessary cut. The count is the maximum number of removable edges.
approaches.insight: Recording a DFS order and accumulating sizes in reverse reproduces post-order without recursion. It is the same O(V) computation, made stack-safe — the pattern to reach for whenever a tree might be deep.

code.python:
def even_forest(self, n: int, edges: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    adj: list[list[int]] = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    parent = [0] * (n + 1)
    order: list[int] = []
    stack = [1]
    parent[1] = 0
    while stack:                          # iterative DFS, no recursion
        u = stack.pop()
        order.append(u)
        for v in adj[u]:
            if v != parent[u]:
                parent[v] = u
                stack.append(v)
    size = [1] * (n + 1)
    cuts = 0
    for u in reversed(order):             # reverse order = post-order
        if u != 1 and size[u] % 2 == 0:
            cuts += 1
        size[parent[u]] += size[u]        # parent[1]=0 → size[0], harmless
    return cuts

java.line: while (!stack.isEmpty()) {            // iterative DFS, no stack overflow
java.explanation: An explicit stack records a DFS order with parents — no recursion depth to overflow.

java.line: for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {    // reverse order = post-order
java.explanation: Processing the order backward guarantees children are summed before their parent.
Even, non-root subtree → its parent edge is a valid cut.
Fold the finished subtree size up into the parent; the root's parent is the unused index 0.

python.line: while stack:                          # iterative DFS, no recursion
python.explanation: Builds the visit order iteratively, safe for deep or skewed trees.

python.line: for u in reversed(order):             # reverse order = post-order
python.explanation: Reverse preorder is a valid post-order: descendants finish before ancestors.
Count a cut for each even non-root subtree.
Accumulate child sizes into the parent; the root dumps into the spare index 0.

pitfalls: Counting the root (index 1) — exclude it explicitly.
Processing the order forward instead of reversed — parents summed before children, wrong sizes.
Forgetting the parent guard while building the order — would revisit via the undirected edge.
Recursive DFS on a long chain — overflow; the explicit stack avoids it.

commonMistakes: Counting the root's subtree, which has no parent edge to remove.
Assuming cuts interfere and reaching for DP when a greedy count suffices.
Recursing on a deep or skewed tree and overflowing the call stack.
Omitting the parent guard, so the undirected edges create a back-and-forth loop.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Counting the root
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The root has no parent edge, so its subtree (the whole tree, size N) can never be separated. Including it overcounts by one whenever N is even — which it always is here.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if size[u] % 2 == 0:        # also counts the root
    cuts += 1
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if u != root and size[u] % 2 == 0:
    cuts += 1

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the parent guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The edges are undirected, so adj[u] includes the parent. Without skipping it, the traversal walks back up and revisits nodes, corrupting subtree sizes (or looping forever).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Deep recursion overflow
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A skewed tree (a chain) has height equal to N. A recursive DFS nests N call frames and can overflow the stack; an explicit-stack iterative DFS keeps that depth on the heap.

patternNote: Subtree-Size DFS with a Greedy Cut Rule. Recognize it when a tree question reduces to a per-node decision based on its subtree count, and the decisions do not interfere. One post-order pass (iterative for safety) yields the sizes; a parity or threshold test yields the answer. The same subtree-size engine powers Diameter, Centroid, and many tree DPs.
